sentences.text: The Inland rules add two river rules here, and they belong together.
Both apply only on the Great Lakes, the Western Rivers, and other waters the Coast Guard specifies.
You saw this in lesson four for narrow channels, and Rule fourteen repeats it.
A power-driven vessel heading downbound with a following current has the right of way over an upbound vessel.
She proposes the manner of passage, and she initiates the maneuvering signals.
On those same waters, a power-driven vessel crossing a river keeps out of the way of a power-driven vessel going up or down it.
It doesn’t matter which side she’s on.
Think of a ferry crossing the Mississippi.
A towboat is coming down the river on the ferry’s port side.
Under the ordinary crossing rule, who would give way?
The towboat would, because the ferry is on her starboard side.
But this is a river, so the ferry keeps clear.
The traffic running the river comes first.
